- s-watchdog-job (the audit's blocker): the core starts the helper in a job that allows breakaway (`ProcessOwner::ComputerHelper` -> JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_BREAKAWAY_OK), so the cursor watchdog can leave the job and foreground actions are no longer refused `computer_cursor_unavailable`. Residual: if the daemon itself sits in a job that forbids breakaway (a service host, a job made by another launcher), the watchdog still cannot start and foreground input fails closed with `computer_cursor_unavailable`. No WMI fallback was ported. Record it if you see it.
- s-shield-ledger: the activation guard writes a `d` ledger line before it disables a self-activating target (Chromium, UWP, WinUI) and an `e` line after it enables it again. `--abort-cleanup` and the elevated worker's supervisor enable a recorded window again. Integration: the elevated worker now records into its own `worker.ledger` in the launch folder. Its supervisor replays only that file, and the parent replays it after the worker exits; anything it cannot clear is handed to the parent's ledger.
- s-helper-eof: the resident helper releases held keys and buttons, the cursor theme and its own foreground lock when stdin ends or it retires. The foreground-lock timeout in focus() is restored by a guard on every return. Integration: the timeout is written back only when the clear succeeded, as in MixWin32Foreground.cs. It is not restored after a panic abort; signing out resets it.
- s-core-crash-cleanup: a helper that exits on its own is cleaned up with `--abort-cleanup` before any respawn, and on end_execution; three `monitor_unresponsive` replies in a row retire the helper; ledgers a dead core left are swept. Integration: every cleanup and recovery holds the backend's turn, so no new helper starts under the same marker while a cleanup runs. `--abort-cleanup` runs are limited to 7 s (Node's ABORT_CLEANUP_TIMEOUT_MS). An unconfirmed dead-helper cleanup at end_execution ends the session. The ledger sweep now runs when the daemon creates its computer pool, not at the first helper start. Only the text "input observation lost (monitor_unresponsive)" counts toward the retire.
- s-screen-input-cleanup: a killed `--screen-input` helper is followed by `mixdog-computer --abort-cleanup` with its marker, and the old remote-screen PS scripts and DLL cache are swept once. Integration: a helper that exits without printing `released` (a crash, or killed from outside) also gets the cleanup. A restart waits for the previous helper's cleanups, so they cannot lift keys the new helper holds. stop() no longer hangs on a helper that never reports its exit.
- s-linux-lines: elevation and pointer-feedback fields go only to the Windows helper. Integration: diagnose sends `ocr_language: null` as Node does. The 3 computer_linux replay tests now pass.

Still open from this round (notes): the dead-helper cleanup is lazy (it runs on the next call, end_execution, release or drop, not the moment the helper exits). Two live cores sharing one data folder would sweep each other's ledgers. A background held pointer gets no button-up after a kill (the reference posts none either). The shield replay compares pid and class, not the thread id. The arrivals baseline is still not taken on a session's first command. The mixdog-spawn service still accepts `computerHelper` from a JSON client.

## What changed in this fix-up that a tester will see

- Captures: window captures come back as JPEG (quality 55) fitted to the capture budget (at most 1280 wide by default). `capture mode=zoom` works on a window frame. State captures of windows with no semantic accessibility carry OCR lines and `[ocr:<frame>:<n>]` elements. A capture that asks for OCR may take up to about 25 s.
- Zoom refuses (never mis-clicks) when the crop is not the region asked for: `stale_frame: native capture did not cut the requested region`, `stale_frame: native capture geometry changed; capture fresh state`, or `coordinate_mismatch: capture dimensions do not match the target coordinate space`.
- Foreground input with no fresh capture is refused: `input_observation_unavailable: capture a fresh foreground-ready observation before input` (also when the last capture is older than 300 s, or carried no input observation).
- Foreground lock: the desktop now has ONE lease owner per process (shared by the core's helpers and the desktop's own workers). Its facts appear in the action reply as `foreground_lock.host` (for example `host.answer: "locked"`), next to the helper's own `foreground_lock.holder`.
- Desktop host on Windows: the desktop's own workers are mixdog-computer.exe (read_only for everything except releasing what they hold). The abort cleanup and the ledger recovery run `mixdog-computer.exe --abort-cleanup`.
- Remote screen (phone control) on Windows: input runs in `mixdog-computer.exe --screen-input`. No powershell.exe, no `remote-screen-host-*.ps1` and no `remote-screen-cache` DLL is created any more (old ones from earlier builds may still sit in the app-data folder; they are unused).
- Paths in replies: a ref scroll on Windows reports `uia_scroll` / "through UIA"; message delivery reports `win32_message`.

## Still unsupported or not ported (expected to fail or be absent)

- `list kind="history"`: still `unsupported` (the core has no action ledger).
- `fill_saved_login` / saved_login from the agent: still `unsupported` at the tool. The helper's check/type steps and the core's fill logic exist, but nothing in the daemon creates the turn-scoped SavedLoginRegistry or routes the action to `fill_saved_login` (no turn id, vault or settlement wiring in compose). Saved-login manual checks can run only once that routing exists.
- Zoom of a display (screen) frame: refused as `stale_frame` (only window frames can be zoomed). No capture-policy (`authorizeCapture`) check on zoom.
- No reserved OCR element budget: an explicit `include_ocr` on a window whose tree fills the element budget reports `OCR skipped: element_budget_exhausted`.
- PowerShell on Windows remains only in the elevated (UAC) launcher of the desktop's own host, which is unreachable now that the desktop host never injects input. No Windows production input path imports `native-source` / `InputTransport.cs` / `host-script.ts` any more (`program.ts` is no longer used by the abort or ledger paths).
- Not ported from reviews (notes, not blockers): the arrivals 1 s watch after an action and the late-read seeding (core-settle-arrivals 1, 4); the recapture-required JSON reply with a fresh observation (core-foreground-lane 5); lane publishing into ComputerSection.lane and user-control-before-recapture order (core-foreground-lane 2, 3); window-transition confirmation, input-recovery verification and timings in replies (core-reply-shaping 4, 5, 6, 8); key guards run before the observation-only refusal (core-keys-guards 1); diagnose probe timeouts of 2.5/3 s and the Windows permissions block (core-policy-targets-diagnose 2, 3); unacknowledged click/key releases are not queued for retry and retries are not bound to the original pid/thread (held-pointer-session-release 2, 3); the cursor watchdog inherits the helper's handles (cursor-presentation 2); the UAC prompt is not bounded inside the helper and the core's 45 s timeout ends long elevated runs (uac-elevated-worker 1); the user_input_active recovery text still says not to call wait_for_user (the TS golden fixture pins that text); frames do not record window/display bounds, so a moved window is caught only when the point leaves it (core-frames-targeting 8); the helper's app backstop for app-only input requests (misc-actions-targets 1; the core resolves app before dispatch).

## 15-minute first check (do this first, in order)

Goal: the smallest set that proves, on a real screen, (A) the helper runs and captures, (B) accessibility is read, (C) background and foreground input land, (D) the foreground lock is taken and reported, (E) the person's input stops automation. Stop at the first failure and keep the reply text.

Running the built helper safely, in isolation. The helper takes over a real keyboard, mouse and cursor, so never run it on a desktop someone is using, and never by double-click: run it only under Mixdog on a dedicated test machine, a second Windows user session that has its own tester-owned windows, or a VM. Windows Sandbox works if you map `D:\mixdog-build\tmp\ft-run` read-only and copy the exe in. Use either the NSIS package built from wincu-int, or an installed Mixdog with `MIXDOG_COMPUTER_BIN` set to a copy of `mixdog-computer-wincu.exe`, set in the environment Mixdog is started from (check in step 1 that Task Manager shows that path). Before you start, close other apps and keep a physical keyboard within reach. Ways out, in order: press Stop on the pill (the helper is killed and `--abort-cleanup` releases its keys and restores windows). If keys still seem stuck, quit Mixdog and start it again: the daemon replays the ledgers left in `<data>/computer/ledgers` at start. Tap Ctrl, Shift, Alt and Win once each. The cursor scheme comes back by itself within 60 s of the helper dying. Signing out resets everything else, including the foreground-lock timeout. If any step reports `computer_cursor_unavailable`, the daemon is in a job that forbids breakaway: stop and record it.

Setup (2 min): install the NSIS package built from wincu-int on the test machine (or set `MIXDOG_COMPUTER_BIN` as above). Open Notepad (empty, title "Untitled - Notepad") on the primary monitor. Open Task Manager > Details, sorted by name. Open Mixdog, make sure Computer Use is enabled and Observation only is off, and keep the Mixdog chat window in front for every step unless a step says otherwise. Ask the agent to run each tool call below exactly and paste the raw reply.

1. Helper and host processes (1 min). Ask: `computer diagnose`.
   Expect: a report for win32 with backend `win32_mixdog_computer_electron` and no error. Task Manager shows `mixdog-computer.exe` under mixdogd. No `powershell.exe` appears at any point in this check.
2. Window list (1 min). Ask: `computer list` (windows).
   Expect: a line for "Untitled - Notepad" with `window_id=hwnd:0x...`, and no Mixdog overlay or pill window in the list. Note the Notepad window_id.
3. Capture and accessibility read (2 min). Ask: `computer capture` mode=state, window_id=<Notepad id>.
   Expect: the text starts `Screenshot of window "Untitled - Notepad" (WxH, N bytes, JPEG quality 55); frame_id=frame-... window_id=hwnd:0x...; coordinates are pixels in this frame`, W is at most 1280, the image shows Notepad correctly (not black, not another window), and the element list contains the editor as a ref (an Edit or Document element named like "Text editor", shown as `[eN]`). Note the frame_id and the editor ref.
4. Background input through a ref, with the foreground lock (2 min). Ask: `computer act` with steps `[{"type":"type","ref":"<editor ref>","text":"mixdog check 1"}]` (default background delivery).
   Expect: "mixdog check 1" appears in Notepad while the Mixdog window stays in front (Notepad never comes forward). The reply row has `ok: true`, `delivery: "background"`, and `effect` confirmed or unverifiable. The reply carries `foreground_lock` with `holder` "worker" or "host"; when it is "host", `foreground_lock.host.answer` is "locked". If `holder` is "none", the reply says activation protection is unavailable: record it as a lock failure.
5. Foreground input with a fresh observation (3 min). Ask: capture Notepad again (as in step 3), then `computer act` with `delivery: "foreground"` and steps `[{"type":"click","frame_id":"<new frame_id>","x":<a point inside the text area>,"y":<same>},{"type":"key","keys":"ctrl+end"},{"type":"type","text":" fg 2"}]`. Keep hands off mouse and keyboard.
   Expect: Notepad comes to the front, the text ends with "mixdog check 1 fg 2", the click landed where the frame point maps (check on the 150% DPI monitor), every row `ok: true` with `delivery: "foreground"`.
6. The person's input stops it (2 min). Capture Notepad again, then ask for a foreground `type` of a 400-character text. While it types, move the physical mouse.
   Expect: typing stops within about one character of the mouse move; the reply has code `user_input_active` and `input_may_have_executed: true`, and the session yields to you. No key stays down: type a few letters yourself in Notepad and they appear normally (no Shift or Ctrl stuck).
7. Clean end (2 min). End the agent's turn (or press Stop on the pill). Click Notepad and the Mixdog window alternately with the mouse.
   Expect: both come to the front normally (no window left non-activatable or disabled), no stuck key or button, and `<data>/computer/ledgers` exists with no non-empty `.ledger` left for a finished hold.
8. Crash recovery (optional, 2 min, test machine only). During a foreground act, end `mixdog-computer.exe` (the resident one, not `--abort-cleanup`) in Task Manager. Expect: the next computer call or the turn's end runs a short-lived `mixdog-computer.exe --abort-cleanup`, no key stays down, and Notepad and Mixdog can both be activated. Then quit Mixdog (or end mixdogd) during a background act and start it again. Expect: no window is left non-activatable after the restart.

Pass = steps 1-7 (step 8 is the extra crash check for the safety fixes). If step 4 shows `holder: "none"` every time, run the full-list items foreground-lock-own and core-lease-relay next.

# Dynamic language servers

Mixdog starts language servers only when a matching file is opened. Resolution order is:

1. Project registry: `.mixdog/lsp.json`
2. Project-local executable: `node_modules/.bin`, `.venv`, or `venv`
3. System `PATH`
4. Monaco and `code_graph` fallback when no server is available

Built-in mappings cover TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, Go, Rust, C/C++/Objective-C, and Ruby. The server process is shared by files that use the same server inside one project and stops after the final document has remained closed for two minutes.

## Project registry

Project configuration is trusted executable configuration, like a project-local MCP stdio server. Review it before opening files from an untrusted repository.

```json
{
  "servers": [
    {
      "id": "typescript-language-server",
      "name": "TypeScript Language Server",
      "languages": ["typescript", "javascript"],
      "command": "typescript-language-server",
      "args": ["--stdio"],
      "candidates": ["node_modules/.bin/typescript-language-server"]
    }
  ]
}
```

`candidates` must be project-relative. A configured server overrides the built-in mapping for its language IDs. Mixdog does not download servers automatically.

# Local HTML preview permissions

Desktop chat links open HTML in the session browser pane, or in the system
browser when no pane is available. The loopback URL is a temporary read
capability, not a grant to the whole directory containing a selected file.

## Access scope

- **Selected file:** a selected-file access token authorizes only that HTML
  file. Neighboring HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, fonts, JSON and CSV are not
  implicitly authorized, even if separately selected or inside a registered
  project. Self-contained HTML is the suitable format for this mode.
- **Registered project:** without a selected-file token, the backend requires
  a registered project. The page can load the existing web-asset types within
  that project, including JSON/CSV. Hidden paths, non-web types and symlinks
  escaping the project remain blocked. Register only a project whose web
  assets you intend its pages to access; do not register a broad personal
  directory just to make a single page's assets load.

The IPC caller cannot supply the scope. An invalid or expired selected-file
permission is rejected, not retried with broader project access. No new folder
picker or automatic grant expansion is introduced. Edit, document preview and
remote-phone APIs are unchanged.

Selected-file HTML receives `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox allow-scripts`.
Inline scripts may render the page, but it is not given the shared loopback
origin's storage/window authority. Forms, popups and downloads are not enabled
by this sandbox policy. This is not an offline mode: external network resources
remain subject to ordinary browser/CORS rules. Use the explicit project scope
for trusted pages requiring same-origin assets or storage.

## Lifetime

Each invocation issues an independent random URL. A file URL is never reused
as, or upgraded to, a project URL for the same folder. The server retains at
most **128 URLs**, evicts the least recently used when full, and expires each
after **one hour**. Only a successfully authorized GET/HEAD refreshes recency;
failed or forbidden requests do not. Recency never extends the absolute expiry.
Click the original chat link again to obtain a fresh URL.

The server rechecks the originating selected-file permission or project
registry on each permitted GET/HEAD, and pins the canonical root/page path.
An explicit denial (removed grant/project, closed owner, or changed canonical
path) invalidates that URL and returns 404. A transient authorization failure
(such as a daemon timeout or path lookup error) returns 503 without disclosing
diagnostics or revoking the lease; retry the same URL after recovery. Uncertainty
never authorizes file bytes. Expiry or revocation during an unsuccessful check
still returns 404, not a retryable response for a dead lease.
Project authority uses the strict store reader: storage/parse failures are not
silently converted to an empty registry. With an older runtime that only has a
tolerant list, absence still denies access but does not prove permanent removal.
Closing the requesting desktop renderer revokes its URLs without revoking
another renderer's previews. Expiry/closure during a pending authorization
cannot revive the URL when that authorization later finishes.

Closing only a browser pane, tab or external browser is not a permission
revocation event in this API; the originating permission checks and hard lease
limit still apply. Revocation blocks subsequent responses, not bytes already
transferred or a response whose transfer has already begun. Files remain live
at their authorized paths, so an ordinary in-place editor replacement stays
visible. This is not an atomic filesystem snapshot against an uncooperative
process replacing paths during the final filesystem checks and open.

## Focused checks

```sh
node scripts/test-direct.mjs src/runtime/shared/projects-authority.test.mjs
npm test --prefix apps/desktop -- src/main/local-page-server.test.mjs src/main/local-page-permissions.test.mjs src/main/local-access-denied.test.mjs
```

The tests exercise real loopback HTTP and temporary files through the public
server and IPC registrar. Project/grant lookups and renderer lifecycle use the
registrar's existing dependency boundaries; the HTTP responses, path checks,
lease table, permission selection and revocation are production code.

# Cycle 1 lightweight conversation compression

Cycle 1 now separates full-source packet construction, compression, validation
and atomic persistence. It does not replace the session-local compaction flow.

- Source bodies are JSON-quoted verbatim. They are not cleaned or clipped at
  400 characters. Packets obey row and estimated-token limits. An oversized row
  is split reversibly; its fragments are never committed as partial source rows.
- Transcript/session ingestion stores the full conversation text after existing
  synthetic-envelope filtering, including code-only and URL-only messages.
  Session replay identity remains compatible with older stored rows. Already
  cleaned legacy DB bodies cannot recover removed code/tables/URLs from a
  chunk repair alone; their original transcript files would be needed.
- Each source packet gets one AI compression call. There is no separate AI
  verification call or quality retry. Oversized inputs still require multiple
  bounded source packets/fragments; this is not a one-call limit per session.
- A packet whose source estimates under 30 tokens stays RAW without an AI call:
  its summary could not be shorter than the rows.
- Code checks fields, valid indexes, duplicates, session isolation and estimated
  token savings. Overlapping/invalid chunks fall back to RAW without discarding
  independent valid chunks. Omitted rows are filled from the source, not retried.
- Accepted roots store `chunk_quality` provenance: validator version, member
  IDs, source/summary hashes, estimated sizes and verification time. Source
  rows are locked and compared again before the metadata transaction commits.
  The record says `structural`, not AI-verified.
- Nonempty rejected/uncompressed rows remain RAW and eligible after cooldown.
  Neither repeated model failures nor an outage retires them as archived.
- Compact memory projection reuses shorter, structurally usable legacy chunks
  without requiring historical verification records. Missing members, known
  stale provenance and overlaps still fall back to originals, including the
  original body stored on the root.
  Compressed bodies omit search metadata and IDs. RAW fallback preserves code,
  tables, URLs and other text that search-oriented cleaning would remove.

`input_token_budget` defaults to 16000 (minimum 4096), with a 2048-token reserve
for prompt overhead. The existing four-window concurrency cap remains. Timing
reports grouping calls, AI time, fetching and persistence. Legacy verification
and retry counters remain zero for comparisons. Token counts are estimates,
not provider billing.

Semantic completeness is not separately verified. A structurally valid summary
can still omit details, including in a reused legacy chunk. This explicitly
trades stricter semantic checking for lower latency and more chunk reuse.
Do not describe resulting compression ratios as proven lossless.

## Existing chunks: snapshot-first audit and simulation

From the repository root:

```powershell
node scripts/memory-chunk-quality.mjs
node scripts/memory-chunk-quality.mjs --input C:\path\snapshot.json --simulate-limit 2
```

The first command reads the advertised running PG service using a repeatable,
read-only transaction. It never starts a service or migrates the live schema.
The second re-chunks original member bodies from a supplied snapshot, using the
configured memory agent. It reports actual elapsed call time and checks exact
source-row coverage of the resulting chunks plus RAW fallback. It changes
neither the live DB nor the supplied snapshot.

Every run allocates a unique temporary directory and retains:

- `snapshot.json`: unchanged source backup.
- `working.json`: separate copy with simulated compressed outputs.
- `report.json`: per-chunk reasons, timings/errors, reuse counts and
  source/projection integrity checks.

Existing summaries passing the cheap checks can be reused without regeneration.
Simulation starts from original member bodies, never from a damaged summary.
Root/member identities and original content are preserved in the working copy.
A provider error stops further AI calls and exits nonzero while
retaining the report. No command here updates the live DB or deploys code.
Legacy deferred/sentinel rows are reported separately and remain available as
RAW; this audit does not silently requeue them.

Run the relevant tests with the repository runner:

```powershell
npm test -- memory-chunk memory-cycle1-quality memory-cycle-packets compact-handoff
```

# Memory maintenance

Conversation history and standing instructions have separate owners:

- **Cycle 1** summarizes conversation by session/topic, keeps source links, and
  generates search embeddings. Default interval: `10m`.
- **Standing memory** is user-curated through `memory` (`add`, `edit`, `delete`,
  `list`), with approval for the exact content and scope. Cycles cannot populate,
  rewrite, merge, or delete these entries.

Manual `flush`, `rebuild` and `backfill` run summarization and embedding
maintenance. The memory tool lists curated records;
use `recall` for generated conversation history.

Public recall supports page sizes up to 100 and offsets up to 500. Internal
retrieval windows cover the requested page, and existing duplicate grouping runs again
after supplemental results and time filters are combined. Embedding and
backfill failures propagate as failures, with committed progress retained in
the result instead of being reported as a successful empty run.

## Existing databases

Stored `duplicate_of` search aliases and concept/lineage links are preserved.
Recall uses these relationships; it does not generate new ones.
A duplicate is collapsed only when its
representative is in the same filtered result, before limits and pagination.
Existing history, summaries and curated
entries are not bulk rewritten or dropped. `pending`/`active`/`archived`
records are all searchable. Archived curated entries remain inactive.
Conflicting CORE keys are preserved and reported; startup defers the
unique index until explicit edits/deletes resolve them. Per-pool locked key
checks prevent new conflicting writes even while that index is deferred.

Session snapshots contain only curated entries.

# Office 검증 실행

변경한 기능을 소유한 테스트만 실행합니다. 일반 코드 수정 때문에 실제 Office 전체 검증을 반복하지 않습니다.

| 명령 | 범위 |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run test:office` | 일반 계약·파일 편집·품질 계산 검증. Microsoft Office를 열지 않습니다. |
| `npm run test:office:render` | 별도 PPTX 렌더 검증. LibreOffice 등 렌더 의존성이 필요합니다. |
| `npm run test:office:live -- excel` | Excel 세션·편집·트랜잭션 |
| `npm run test:office:live -- word` | Word 세션·편집 |
| `npm run test:office:live -- powerpoint` | PowerPoint 편집·저장·다시 열기·슬라이드 가져오기 |
| `npm run test:office:live -- author` | PPTX 재작성 시 세션 재사용 |
| `npm run test:office:live -- attach` | 열린 Excel 문서의 정확한 연결 |
| `npm run test:office:live -- contract` | 실제 Office와 portable 백엔드의 스냅샷 호환성 |
| `npm run test:office:compat` | 매크로·서식 9종 전체 호환성 |
| `npm run test:office:live:all` | 모든 라이브 검증. 전체 검증이 필요한 경우에만 선택합니다. |

라이브 명령에 범위를 주지 않으면 도움말만 표시하고 Office를 실행하지 않습니다.
라이브 검증에는 Windows와 Microsoft Office가 필요하며, 일부 검증은 실제 창을 사용합니다.
여러 라이브 검증을 동시에 실행하지 않습니다. 출력은 완료 때까지 모으지 않고 즉시 전달합니다.

기존 파일·테스트 이름 지정 방식도 지원합니다.

```powershell
npm run test:office:live -- src/runtime/office/office-live-runtime.test.mjs 're-authoring a deck'
```

`compat`은 `docm`, `dotm`, `dotx`, `xltx`, `xltm`, `xlsm`, `pptm`, `potx`, `potm`을 모두 검사합니다.
각 형식의 결과가 별도로 표시됩니다. 검사 자체를 삭제하거나 임의 표본으로 대체하지 않습니다.

실패한 검사는 전체 로그를 보존하고 원인을 확인한 뒤, 수정한 범위만 다시 실행합니다.
이미 통과한 검사는 관련 변경이 없는 한 반복하지 않습니다.

# Remote whole-PC screen source

Stage 2 of the phone remote control: the paired phone sees and operates the
maintainer's whole PC screen, like a remote-desktop app, over the WebRTC
transport (`docs/remote-webrtc.md`). This page covers the `screen` source:
capture, input injection, the secure-desktop/UAC switch, and the
permission/safety model. `webrtc-pc-side` owns the peer connection, signaling
and phone UI. This source plugs into them through the
`RemoteWebrtcVideoSource` adapter described below.

The source uses the contract's `{ kind: 'screen', screenId }`. A host that
serves it advertises the same `browserWebrtc` capability. A phone lists the
displays, picks one, and streams it the same way it streams a browser page.

## Files

| File | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `apps/desktop/src/shared/remote-screen.ts` | Screen-only helpers on top of the contract: the `KeyboardEvent.code` → virtual-key/scan-code table (`remoteScreenKeyForCode`) and `openRemoteScreenCaptureTrack` (opens the sender's track from a capture plan). |
| `apps/desktop/src/main/remote-screen/screen-geometry.ts` | Display enumeration (`summarizeScreenDisplay` → the contract's `RemoteScreenDisplaySummary`), the locked video geometry (native pixels, capped and even), the video-pixel → desktop-pixel pointer map (multi-monitor, DPI), and fitting a helper frame onto that geometry. |
| `apps/desktop/src/main/remote-screen/screen-input-host.ts` | The Windows input/UAC-watcher helper process. It injects desktop input through Computer Use's own checked `SendInput` transport and watches the input desktop and `consent.exe`/`LogonUI`. It also holds the temp-file sweep. |
| `apps/desktop/src/main/remote-screen/screen-input-dispatch.ts` | A pure mapper. It turns a viewer's `RemoteScreenInput` into host commands at the acknowledged geometry generation (`screenInputCommands`) and defines each press's identity and its release (`holdKeyOf`, `isHoldDown`, `releaseCommandFor`). It keeps no state. |
| `apps/desktop/src/main/remote-screen/screen-input-router.ts` | `ScreenInputRouter`: the single serialized, cancellable path for input, backend switches and releases of one session. It tracks held presses per backend + origin + key and releases them at the session's defined points. |
| `apps/desktop/src/main/remote-screen/secure-desktop-switch.ts` | The pure decision: ordinary capture, an elevation prompt that can't take remote input, the installed helper, or a blocked secure desktop. Also builds the status pushed to the phone. |
| `apps/desktop/src/main/remote-screen/screen-source.ts` | `RemoteScreenSource`, one per viewer: start/stop, geometry, capture plan, frames, input, live re-authorization, the secure-desktop switch, the indicator and the log. |
| `apps/desktop/src/main/remote-screen/screen-webrtc-source.ts` | `createScreenWebrtcSource`: adapts a `RemoteScreenSource` to the WebRTC host's `RemoteWebrtcVideoSource` (`main/remote-webrtc/source.ts`). |
| `apps/desktop/src/main/remote-screen/screen-webrtc-sources.ts` | The window process's screen sessions for the WebRTC host: per-connection access, resolve, close (see "Main wiring"). |
| `apps/desktop/src/main/remote-screen/screen-access-publisher.ts` | Service side: sends each relay connection's access (grant / deny) to the window. |
| `apps/desktop/src/main/remote-screen/screen-electron.ts` | Electron pieces: displays with capture ids, the input host factory, the on-PC indicator (the remote-control pill). |
| `apps/desktop/src/main/remote-screen/secure-desktop-adapter.ts` | Adapts the real secure-desktop client (`main/secure-desktop/`, protocol v4) to the switch's `SecureDesktopClient` interface, plus the grant, lock-state and issue surface. |
| `apps/desktop/src/main/remote-screen/secure-desktop-helper.ts` | `SecureDesktopHelper`: the adapter every session shares, rebuilt after an install, plus the install state and the phone's install request (see "Helper install and control grants"). |
| `apps/desktop/src/main/remote-screen/screen-selfcheck.mjs` | A local self-check that needs no phone and doesn't touch the cursor. It runs no capture and injects nothing; input goes through a recording backend. |

## Contract fold-in

The screen wire types belong to the shared contract
`apps/desktop/src/shared/remote-webrtc.ts`, owned by `webrtc-pc-side`. This
module imports them and no longer defines its own copies:

- `RemoteScreenButton`, `RemoteScreenKey`, `RemoteScreenInput`,
  `parseRemoteScreenInput`, `MAX_REMOTE_SCREEN_TEXT`;
- `RemoteScreenHelperState`, `RemoteScreenStatus`, `RemoteScreenStopReason`;
- `RemoteScreenCapturePlan`, `remoteScreenCaptureConstraints`;
- `RemoteScreenDisplaySummary`, used by `screen-geometry.ts`;
- the data-channel messages: the `screen-input` member of
  `RemoteWebrtcChannelFromClient`, validated by
  `parseRemoteWebrtcChannelFromClient`, and the desktop pushes
  (`RemoteWebrtcChannelPush`): the status `RemoteWebrtcScreenStatusMessage`
  and the cursor `RemoteWebrtcScreenCursorMessage`, read on the phone by
  `readRemoteWebrtcScreenStatus` and `readRemoteWebrtcScreenCursor`.

`remoteScreenKeyForCode` and `openRemoteScreenCaptureTrack` stay in
`shared/remote-screen.ts`. The `screen-input` control is a `RemoteScreenInput`:

- `screen-pointer`: `move`, or `down`/`up` with `left|right|middle`. x/y are in
  video pixels of the locked geometry. Multi-monitor mapping happens on the
  desktop side.
- `screen-wheel`: x/y plus WheelEvent-signed deltas in Windows wheel units.
- `screen-key`: `down`/`up` by virtual key + scan code + extended flag.
- `screen-keys`: `{ keys: RemoteScreenKey[] }`, an atomic combo: 1 to
  `MAX_REMOTE_SCREEN_COMBO_KEYS` (8) distinct keys, pressed in order and
  released in reverse as one router step (`ScreenInputRouter.dispatchKeys`).
  The same control check gates each press and the same press tracking
  applies: a release point between steps still finds them. Whatever the
  combo pressed is released even if it stops early (control lost, a cancel,
  a failed send); a key the session already holds (a modifier the phone
  keeps down) is neither pressed nor released. A combo types no text, so the
  AltGr text rule doesn't apply to it; a combo that includes AltGr's keys
  presses them like any others. Acked `applied` only when every key went
  down and up.
- `screen-text`: literal Unicode, bounded by `MAX_REMOTE_SCREEN_TEXT`.
- `screen-release`: lift every key and button this viewer holds.

Desktop → phone on the same channel (not input-acked, not epoch-bound):

- `screen-status`: `{ v, kind: 'screen-status', status: RemoteScreenStatus }`,
  pushed on every status change (from the source's `onStatus`), including the
  final `stopped`. `status.helper` is `not-needed | active | starting |
  missing | failed | in-use` (`failed`: an installed service that could not
  be started; `in-use`: another viewer's session holds the helper, see "One
  holder"). `status.helperInfo` (`RemoteScreenHelperInfo`, required) is
  the secure-desktop helper block: `offer` (`'install' | 'update' | 'none'`),
  `outcome` (this session's last install request: `installed | updated |
  declined | failed | in-progress | other-user | unavailable`, or null),
  `detail` (its diagnostic, at most `MAX_REMOTE_SCREEN_HELPER_DETAIL` = 256
  characters, or null), `issue` (`grant_key_missing | grant_expired |
  input_failed | desktop_unavailable | sas_disabled_by_policy`, or null) and
  `secure` (`'lock' | 'uac' | null`), and the optional `accountIsAdmin`
  (boolean: whether the PC's signed-in account is an administrator; absent
  when not told, which an older PC never does); see "Helper install and
  control grants".
- `screen-helper-challenge`: `{ v, kind: 'screen-helper-challenge', epoch,
  nonce, challenge }`, a helper grant challenge to sign for video run
  `epoch`. Built by `remoteWebrtcScreenHelperChallenge`, read on the phone by
  `readRemoteWebrtcScreenHelperChallenge`. Never in the promotion snapshot.
- `screen-cursor`: `{ v, kind: 'screen-cursor', x, y, generation }`, the PC
  cursor in whole video pixels of geometry `generation`. The cursor stays
  baked into the video; this only anchors trackpad mode. It is sampled
  through the input host's cursor read-back (physical desktop pixels, the
  pointer mapping's space) once per capture frame interval,
  `1000 / maxFrameRate` ms (30 fps → 34 ms): the video shows at most
  `maxFrameRate` pictures a second, so a position sampled more often can't
  match a frame the phone shows, and one per frame keeps the anchor at most
  a frame behind. It is pushed only when it changed, only while the cursor
  is on the viewed display, and not while the helper serves the secure
  desktop (the host can't read the cursor there, and a normal-desktop
  position doesn't match the helper's picture). The switch to the helper
  clears the cached position, a read still in flight across that switch
  (or across a new geometry) is dropped when it completes, and the
  promotion snapshot carries no cursor while the helper serves.
- `screen-video`: `{ v, kind: 'screen-video', epoch, path }`, `epoch` a
  positive integer increasing per session and unique across sessions (one
  helper-wide counter; it is also the epoch the helper is given, see "What
  guarantees revocation"), `path` `'capture' | 'helper'`: video
  run `epoch` of that path is on the track from now on (see "Video runs and
  control"). Read with `readRemoteWebrtcScreenVideo`.
- All of them go only to a channel that is up (`promoting` or `webrtc`); a
  viewer's channel gets the current status, the current video run (once
  announced) and the last cursor once when it is promoted
  (`RemoteWebrtcVideoSource.channelState`), so nothing sent before is missed.

Phone → desktop, not input (never acked, never gated by the input epoch):

- `screen-frame-seen`: `{ v, kind: 'screen-frame-seen', epoch }`, validated by
  `parseRemoteWebrtcChannelFromClient`. The phone sends it once per run: for
  the first frame it presents (`requestVideoFrameCallback`) whose
  `metadata.receiveTime` is later than the arrival of that run's
  `screen-video`. A phone whose frame metadata has no `receiveTime` does not
  send it (no control on the helper path, the safe default). On a browser
  source it is a contract violation. The receipt identifies the announced
  run, not the provenance of the presented pixels (see "Video runs and
  control" for the accepted limits).
- `screen-helper-grant`: `{ v, kind: 'screen-helper-grant', epoch, challenge,
  signature }`, the phone's answer to a `screen-helper-challenge`; the phone
  builds the text with `encodeRemoteWebrtcScreenHelperGrant`.
- `screen-helper-install`: `{ v, kind: 'screen-helper-install', publicKey }`,
  install or update the helper enrolling this controller key; the phone builds
  the text with `encodeRemoteWebrtcScreenHelperInstall`.
- Either may carry `credential: { password, user? }` (the phone's Windows
  password, no UAC prompt on the PC; see "PC access") and the install also
  `keys`; `screen-helper-enroll` (`{ v, kind, publicKey, credential? }`) is
  read by `readRemoteWebrtcScreenHelperEnroll` where
  `parseRemoteWebrtcChannelFromClient` refuses it, and is handled like the
  install.
- All are validated on the PC and are a
  contract violation on a browser source. Encodings: `nonce`, `challenge` (16
  bytes) and `signature` (64-byte P-256 `r ‖ s`) are canonical padded base64,
  the helper's own wire encoding and what `signSecureDesktopGrant`
  (`shared/secure-desktop-grant.ts`) takes and returns, so nothing is
  re-encoded on either side; `publicKey` is unpadded base64url of the 65-byte
  uncompressed point (`isSecureDesktopControllerKey`). `epoch` is a positive
  integer.

## Capture

Chosen approach: Electron's `desktopCapturer` plus a `getUserMedia`
`chromeMediaSource: 'desktop'` MediaStream in the hidden sender renderer (owned
by the WebRTC side), opened with `openRemoteScreenCaptureTrack` from the
source's `capturePlan()`. The size is pinned to the display's native pixels.
Why:

- **Latency/CPU.** The renderer path hands a live `MediaStreamTrack` straight
  to the `RTCPeerConnection`. The encoder reads frames with no main↔renderer
  pixel copy and no JS framebuffer. A frame source fed from main costs a
  full-frame copy every frame. It is only worth it where the renderer can't
  reach, which is the secure desktop, handled by the helper below.
- **Multi-monitor.** `desktopCapturer.getSources({ types: ['screen'] })` lists
  one source per display. The phone picks by `screenId`, and the plan carries
  that display's `captureSourceId`.
- **DPI.** Geometry uses the display's physical pixels, and capture is pinned
  to them. A monitor scaled to 150 % streams and maps at its true resolution.
- **Cursor.** Chromium's desktop capturer draws the cursor into the frames.

Geometry is locked when the stream starts. A new generation is created only
when the display is removed or its native size changes. It is announced through
`onGeometry`, which the adapter forwards to the sink. A display change that
keeps the same size does not restart capture. When the chosen display is
removed, the session stops.

## Input injection

Input reuses Mixdog's existing native `SendInput` backend; there is no new
injector. On the ordinary desktop, a small resident Windows helper
(`screen-input-host.ts`) embeds the Computer Use input transport
(`InputTransport.cs` `MixNativeInput`) unchanged. That gives it the same checked
delivery, foreign-input guard and ownership receipt the agent uses. It is a
separate process with its own `dwExtraInfo` marker, kept apart from the agent's
worker pool.

- **Absolute pointer per monitor.** `mapScreenPointer` turns video pixels into
  virtual-screen desktop pixels (negative on monitors left of or above the
  primary). The helper sends them as `MOUSEEVENTF_ABSOLUTE | VIRTUALDESK`. It is
  per-monitor DPI aware.
- **Stale geometry.** Moves, presses and wheel events at a stale geometry
  generation are dropped. A button-up always maps (released in place), so a
  press made before a geometry change can still be lifted.
- **Keys.** Sent by virtual key and set-1 scan code, with
  `KEYEVENTF_EXTENDEDKEY` where needed. The phone gets both from
  `KeyboardEvent.code` via `remoteScreenKeyForCode`.
- **Unicode text.** Sent through `KEYEVENTF_UNICODE`, paced like the agent's
  text entry. Tab and line breaks are sent as real Tab/Enter keys, not Unicode
  packets. Modifiers the session holds decide how text is typed:
  - none held, or only Shift: typed as is;
  - **AltGr** (Right Alt, alone or with the Left Ctrl Windows adds beside it):
    the session's own AltGr keys are lifted, the text is typed as Unicode, and
    the keys are pressed again. The target sees plain characters and the
    phone's held state is unchanged. If the text fails, the keys are still
    pressed again. The live gate (cancel generation + authorization) is
    checked before the text and before every re-press. Once a stop, unpair or
    disconnect lands, nothing positive is sent: no text, and no modifier is
    pressed again. The keys already lifted are up and no longer held; only
    the ones not yet lifted stay held, for the release that follows. All
    AltGr keys must have been pressed on the current desktop identity, or the
    text is refused. That origin is rechecked against the backend's identity
    before every lift, before the text and before every re-press, so every
    lift, the text and every re-press land only on the session + desktop the
    keys were pressed on. Once the identity changes, nothing more is sent from
    this text command: no further lift, no text, no re-press. The keys already
    lifted are up; the ones not yet lifted are dropped and counted, like any
    release whose desktop is unreachable. (A lift already in flight when the
    identity changes was sent while it still matched; it can't be recalled.);
  - any other Ctrl, Alt or Win (for example Ctrl+Left Alt, or AltGr plus Win):
    the text is **refused**, so it can't fire a shortcut. It is not queued or
    retried; the input is acked as not applied.

### The input router

`ScreenInputRouter` is the only path any input, backend switch or release takes
to a desktop. There are two backends: `desktop` (the input host) and `secure`
(the secure-desktop helper).

- **Serialized.** Input, switches and releases run strictly in order, one at a
  time, so a release always follows the in-flight command it undoes.
- **Holds per backend, with origin.** Every press is held by the backend that
  injected it and tagged with its **origin**: the Windows session id and the
  desktop it landed on. Each backend reports this through `identity()`:
  - the input host: its session (sent in its `ready` line) plus the input
    desktop's object name, lower-cased (e.g. `default`), from its watcher;
  - the helper: the `session` and the desktop's real object name from
    `server-hello` / `desktop-changed`, lower-cased like the input host's.

  Presses are keyed by **backend + origin + key**. Pressing the same key
  again under a new origin (for example `default`, then `winlogon`) creates a
  second entry. A press is only made while the identity is known, and it is
  recorded before it is sent, so a press whose delivery is uncertain still
  gets released. Its release goes back only through that backend and only
  while that backend reports the same session and desktop. It never goes
  through whichever backend is active now, and never to a helper that
  reconnected to another session or desktop. An up for a press the backend
  doesn't hold on its current desktop is skipped.

  **Desktop names.** These are compared as reported (case-insensitively). The
  helper reports the desktop's real object name, so the lock screen, sign-in
  and UAC consent are all `winlogon`; two different names are distinct
  desktops, and a press made under one is not released under the other.
- **Release points.** `releaseAll()` releases every press of every backend.
  `switchTo(next)` first releases the old backend's presses through the old
  backend, then makes `next` active. Activating or deactivating the helper
  happens inside the same queue step (`before`/`after` hooks), so the switch is
  atomic relative to input. A press its backend can't release at that moment
  (it reports another desktop or none, or the send fails or is abandoned) is
  **dropped** and counted through `onDropped`; nothing is retried later.
- **Cancel generation.** `cancel()` bumps a generation counter. Queued input
  from an earlier generation is rejected when its turn comes. A plan with
  several commands also stops between commands when the generation changes or
  the `allowed()` gate turns false (re-read when its turn comes and before each
  command). Releases are never cancelled.
- **Idempotent.** `releaseAll()` with nothing held sends nothing.
- **Abandon.** `abandon()` fails every in-flight backend call (sends and the
  helper-activation hooks of a switch) at once, and every later one
  immediately, so the releases that follow are dropped and counted.

### Key-release guarantee

The guarantee is the standard remote-desktop level (the RustDesk approach):
presses are tracked per session and released at defined points. There is no
durable recovery across sessions or restarts.

**Released.** Everything the session holds is released, through the backend
that pressed it and only onto the session + desktop it landed on, at each of:
phone disconnect or viewer leave, demote, unpair, a backend switch (before
the switch), stop, and app quit.

**Dropped.** If that backend or desktop is unreachable at that moment (the
input desktop changed, the helper reconnected elsewhere, the injector died or
missed the stop deadline), the release is **dropped** and its count logged
(`release-dropped`, per backend, never key identities). No debt outlives the
moment, or the session.

So keys are released at every defined exit while the injector is reachable.
If the app or the helper is killed, or the target desktop is unreachable at
that moment, a held key may stay down until the user presses it again on the
PC. This matches common remote-desktop apps.

### Shutdown

**Stop.** `stop()` does its synchronous part at once (capture off, indicator
hidden, queued input cancelled) and starts a **watchdog** in the same call,
independent of what the input queue is waiting on. The release step is queued
behind the in-flight command, so it undoes it. If the watchdog fires first,
the input host is killed and the router is abandoned, so a backend that
stopped answering can't hold the stop open; the releases not yet sent are
dropped and counted. Then the backends close.

The watchdog defaults to one command's acknowledgment deadline
(`COMMAND_TIMEOUT_MS`, below). A responsive backend completes the whole release
well within the time one command may take. `stop(reason, { deadlineMs })`
replaces that bound for one stop. A later `stop` with a shorter `deadlineMs`
moves the running stop's absolute deadline earlier and re-arms it, both
during the release step and while the host closes; it never moves it later.
The same deadline also bounds closing the host: its graceful stop gets
whatever time is left and is killed when none is. `released()` therefore
resolves within the stop's deadline.

**Command acknowledgment deadline (host).** Every command to the input host
must be acknowledged within `COMMAND_TIMEOUT_MS`, imported from
`apps/desktop/src/main/computer/backend/worker-requests.ts`. That is Computer
Use's per-command ceiling for the same PowerShell host round trip through the
same `MixNativeInput` transport; no new number is introduced. A helper that
misses it is killed: anything it did later would be out of order with the
releases that follow. Killing it fails every pending command and fires
`onExit`, which stops a live session with reason `error`.

**What a kill does to held keys.** The helper's own release-on-quit
(`ReleaseOwned` on `q` or end of stdin) runs only on a graceful exit. A killed
helper (TerminateProcess) runs nothing, and **Windows does not lift input a
killed process injected**: a key or button it pressed stays down in the system
key state until a matching up is injected (or the user presses and releases
it). So after a kill the session never assumes anything was released: every
press it held, including one whose down was cut off mid-delivery, is dropped
and counted, and may stay down until the user presses it again.

**Late key-ups: physical-key risk.** A release point's key-up can land some
time after the press it undoes, for example a release queued behind a slow
command, or a demote long after the press. Matching the origin only rules
out the wrong session or desktop. It does **not** prove that nobody pressed
the key on that desktop in the meantime. If the user is physically holding
the same key on the PC when the key-up arrives, that up **releases the key the
user is holding**. Nothing detects a local, physical press in between: the
Computer Use transport has a foreign-key guard (`RecordForeignKey` /
`BeginOwnershipObservation` in `InputTransport.cs`), but this host never feeds
it. Closing this needs local key observation (for example a low-level
keyboard hook that records foreign presses), and that is not implemented.

**At app quit.** `stopScreenSourcesForQuit(sessions)` stops every session at
once with `deadlineMs: SCREEN_QUIT_BUDGET_MS` (a session already stopping is
shortened to it), so quit takes at most 5000 ms however many sessions run.
That is Windows' hung-app timeout: how long Windows waits for an application
to end before it treats it as not responding
(`HKCU\Control Panel\Desktop\HungAppTimeout`, default 5000 ms;
[HungAppTimeout](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-2000-server/cc978614(v=technet.10)).
The Restart Manager uses the same value for forced shutdown:
[RM_SHUTDOWN_TYPE](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/restartmanager/ne-restartmanager-rm_shutdown_type).)
`COMMAND_TIMEOUT_MS` stays the normal per-command deadline. The quit call
site is `disposeDesktopResources` in `apps/desktop/src/main/index.ts`: it
calls `browserHost.stopRemoteScreens()` (→ `stopScreenSourcesForQuit`) first
and waits for it beside the rest of the teardown, so the 4 s teardown bound
doesn't cut the 5 s release budget short. Disposing the browser host (its
window closing) stops the sessions the same way. Either call first latches
the screen sources closed for good (see "Main wiring"), so no session opens
during or after the quit.

### Helper channel and temp files

- **Who can command the helper.** Only the app that spawned it. The line
  protocol runs over the child's own stdin/stdout pipes. It opens no named
  pipe, socket or window, so no other process or account can reach it.
- **Greeting.** The helper writes its first `desktop` line, then
  `ready <windows session id>`. Both the desktop and the session are known when
  `start()` resolves, so the first press can carry its origin.
- **Liveness.** Every command carries the acknowledgment deadline above, and a
  helper that misses one is killed. `kill()` ends it without the
  release-on-quit; the session drops its presses and logs the count.
- **Files.** `publishProgram` writes a unique bootstrap script per process,
  `remote-screen-host-<pid>-<random>.ps1`, with mode 0o600, removed when the
  host exits. Next to it, the compiled assembly is cached per build in
  `remote-screen-cache/remote-screen-host-<build>.dll`. The directory must be
  an owner-only app-data folder (same model as the agent host). The cached
  assembly is loaded without further checks, so a folder another account can
  write to would let it plant code into the injector.
- **Sweep.** Every publish runs `sweepScreenHostFiles` first. It removes
  scripts whose process is dead, assemblies from other builds, and compile
  staging files (`...dll.<pid>.tmp`) whose process is dead. Files of live
  processes and of the current build are kept. Crashed hosts don't leave
  orphaned `remote-screen-host-*` files behind.

## Secure desktop / UAC

A LocalSystem service + session helper (`native/mixdog-secure-desktop/`)
captures and injects on the secure desktop; its TS client is
`apps/desktop/src/main/secure-desktop/`. `secure-desktop-switch.ts` imports no
helper implementation. It depends only on the `SecureDesktopClient` interface
and decides the source as a pure function. `secure-desktop-adapter.ts` adapts
the real client to that interface (`index.ts` plugs it in):

- **Not installed:** the adapter is `NO_SECURE_DESKTOP` (not installed), so a
  secure desktop stays blocked until the paired phone asks for the install
  (see "Helper install and control grants").
- **Connection:** dialled on the first `setActive(true)` (not awaited, so the
  input queue never waits on it); a wanted activation is sent once the
  handshake completes. While activation is wanted, a lost or refused
  connection is dialled again after 1 s, doubling to 30 s, reset by a
  success. Connect, desktop change and disconnect all fire
  `onDesktopChanged`, which re-runs the decision.
- **Identity:** `session()` and `desktop()` come from the client's
  `session()` object (`{protocol, version, session, desktop}`), current
  through `desktop-changed`.
- **Input:** host commands become the protocol's `InputEvent` in the same
  desktop pixels. A button without a position uses the last one sent (the
  helper releases in place). The cursor read-back has no helper counterpart
  and is refused. `sendInput` settles within the client's own deadline.
- **Dispose:** the screen sources own the adapter and call `dispose()` when
  they close (browser host dispose or app quit), once every session
  released, since those releases may go through the helper. It cancels the
  reconnect, detaches its listeners from the client and closes the
  connection, also one still in its handshake; a connect that succeeds
  anyway is closed when it does. Nothing dials after it.

The decision:

- **Lock screen vs UAC.** Both are on the one `Winlogon` desktop. The
  helper's WTS lock state (`locked()`) decides whenever it reports one,
  before the local `LogonUI` check (LogonUI also draws an unlocked session's
  Ctrl+Alt+Del screen): locked is `lock`; not locked is `uac` while
  `consent.exe` runs, else `secure`. Without a lock state (unknown, or the
  helper not connected) LogonUI means `lock`, as before. On the readable
  desktop an unlocked session's LogonUI is no prompt at all. A change of the
  lock state alone arrives as `desktop-changed`.
- **Secure desktop up.** The input-desktop watcher can't open the input
  desktop, or the desktop is `winlogon`. That covers UAC on the secure desktop,
  Ctrl+Alt+Del, and the lock/sign-in screen. If the helper is installed and
  attached, its frames and input take over: the router switches to `secure`.
  The old desktop's presses are released through the input host first, and
  dropped (counted) when it can no longer reach that desktop.
  **No blind control:** on the helper path control waits until the helper's
  video actually reaches the viewer. The sender reports it through
  `setHelperVideo(true)`; until then the status is `secure-desktop` with
  `control: false` (the phone shows its blocked state) and the router
  refuses every positive input. `setHelperVideo(false)` withdraws control at
  once and releases what the viewer holds through the helper. Leaving the
  helper path clears the report, so each helper period needs its own, and a
  report outside it counts for nothing. Releases always go through. The
  screen's WebRTC adapter reports it once the current video run was both
  delivered into the track and seen by the phone (see "Video runs and
  control" below). Without the helper, the
  phone gets a `secure-desktop` state ("elevation prompt on the PC — approve
  there or install the helper"), never a frozen or black frame.
- **Elevation prompt on the ordinary desktop.** `consent.exe` is running while
  the input desktop can still be read. The live view keeps working, but the
  prompt doesn't accept remote input without the helper. Control is withheld
  and an `elevation-prompt` state is shown. A connected helper is kept warm so
  a jump to the secure desktop is seamless.
- **Helper frames.** They are fitted to the locked geometry and emitted only
  while the live permission allows viewing. Malformed frames are dropped.
  The helper captures the whole virtual screen with GDI at most every 66 ms,
  and only once its previous frame was written out (`CAPTURE_INTERVAL` in
  `native/mixdog-secure-desktop/src/helper.rs`; ipc-spec "Capture approach").
- **Deactivation.** When the desktop returns, the router switches back to
  `desktop`. The helper's presses are released through the helper first, then
  it is deactivated.

### Helper install and control grants

**Install on demand** (`secure-desktop-helper.ts`). The screen sources hold a
`SecureDesktopHelper`: the current adapter plus the install state and request;
each session sees it through its own `SecureDesktopLease` (`lease()`, let go
once the session released). The phone's `screen-helper-install` reaches
`RemoteScreenSource.requestHelperInstall` (running and paired only), which
checks the install state for the phone's key, then calls the installer's
`request(publicKey)` (main/secure-desktop/install-request.ts: at most one UAC
prompt, joining a request already running; nothing is single-flighted here).

- **No prompt after a refusal.** One UAC prompt per phone request, and no
  retry after the PC refused: a `declined` outcome latches in the helper
  (PC side, every session), and from then on each install request answers
  `declined` with the detail `DECLINED_ON_PC` ("refused on the PC; restart
  Mixdog on the PC before asking again") and launches nothing. An app
  restart clears it (the helper lives with the main window); it stands in
  for the local action on the PC that should clear it, without a settings
  UI for now.
The result lands in the status: `outcome`, `detail` (cut to 256 characters),
and the offer from its install state, which is relative to the phone's key.
A request that rejects (the bridge could not be run) reports `failed` with
its message. An answer to a request (or check) after a later one of the
session started counts for nothing.

- **Offer.** Each session start checks the install state without a key
  (the phone names its key only when it asks) and maps it with
  `installOfferFor`: `not-installed` → `install`, `outdated` → `update`
  (also a helper enrolled with no key or another phone's, once the phone's
  own request checked relative to its key), anything else → `none`. Before
  the check answers it is `none`.
- **Rebuilt after an install, only when it changed.** A client reads the
  install state (its secret) once, when it is built, so an `installed` or
  `updated` outcome builds a fresh client and adapter, as install-request.ts
  requires, but only when the install changed: not when the state for the
  phone's key was already `installed` (current, enrolling that key) before
  the request and the adapter knows an install (the installer answers
  `installed` then without a prompt), and not when the adapter was rebuilt
  since the request began (a request another session joined ends with the
  same install; a rebuild by a state check happens only once an install is
  there). So does a check that reads `installed` while the adapter reports
  not installed (an install that finished after its request had answered
  `in-progress`). The swap keeps every listener, applies the holder's
  activation and declared run to the new adapter, fires `onDesktopChanged`
  so each session re-decides, and disposes the old one.

**One holder** (helper ownership). The helper serves one session at a time,
so several sessions (phones, displays) can't invalidate each other's runs
and grants:

- The session that activates it first holds it. Only the holder's video
  runs are declared, only its grants and input reach the helper, and only
  it hears the helper's frames, challenges and issues.
- Another session that needs the helper meanwhile reads `ownedElsewhere()`
  and decides through the switch's `helperOwnedElsewhere`: status
  `helper: 'in-use'` with no control (blocked on the secure desktop, an
  un-actionable prompt in place), its runs not declared, its grants
  dropped (`sendGrant` refuses), its input refused, and no challenge of
  the helper's reaches its phone. It waits, in the order it asked.
- The hold passes when the holder deactivates the helper (its switch, after
  its presses were released through it) or its session ends (the stop
  deactivates it; the lease is let go once it released): to the first
  waiting session or, with nobody waiting, the helper is deactivated.
  Every session re-decides when the holder changes.

**What guarantees revocation.** A declaration alone does not: the helper
ends its grant on `video-run` only when the epoch differs from its current
one; re-declaring the same epoch changes nothing (`GrantBook::set_epoch`,
native/mixdog-secure-desktop/src/security.rs). Two things do:

- **Deactivation, on every handover.** Taking the hold is always, in this
  order on the one connection: control off (on a handover: the helper
  releases everything it holds and revokes its live grant and every open
  challenge, helper.rs), the new holder's fresh run declared (`onHold`:
  its screen adapter starts a new run on the path it is on, minted and
  declared), control on (a challenge for the new epoch is due at once).
  Nothing of the new holder reaches the helper before the revoke, and
  nothing of the previous one counts after it, whatever the epochs.
- **Epochs unique app-wide.** Every run of every session takes its epoch
  from one helper-wide counter that only rises (`mintVideoRun`, through the
  source's `nextVideoRun`), so no two sessions' runs share one. The run is
  also what the phone is shown (`screen-video`, its challenges) and signs:
  the phone signs only a challenge whose epoch is the run it was shown
  (remote-screen-helper.ts), so the helper epoch and the run are one
  number rather than a mapping.

The lease mirrors the helper's gate so nothing is relayed that the helper
would have to refuse: a grant passes only from the holder, for the epoch it
declared in this hold, naming a challenge forwarded to it since (the
latest 4: one every 2 s, each kept through an age of 6 s inclusive), each
challenge once; the holder's
input passes only once such a grant was relayed. A rebuilt adapter (a new
connection) starts over. The helper stays the authority on a grant's
lifetime.

**Stopped service** (after a reboot the service is registered but stopped).
A lease's `ensureRunning` calls the installer's `ensureRunning()`:
an unelevated start with no prompt, for a current install only. Sessions
asking together share one attempt, and a connected helper needs none. A
session asks at start when its install-state check reads `installed` and
the helper isn't connected, and each time it activates the helper while not
connected (the moment the helper is needed). The answer re-decides through
the switch's `helperServiceDown`: installed but not running (or a start that
rejected) is status `helper: 'failed'`; a running answer is `starting` again
(the adapter, dialling while activation is wanted, reaches it on its next
reconnect); a connection is `active` whatever was answered. An answer after
a later attempt started counts for nothing.

**Control grants** (helper protocol v4, ipc-spec "Control grants"). The
helper injects only under a grant the paired phone signed:

- **Runs.** Every video run of the holder is declared to the helper with
  `setVideoRun` (the first once the session runs, each later one when it
  starts: path change, watchdog stall, lost channel, and a fresh one when
  the session takes the hold). A run of a new epoch ends the helper's live
  grant, so a grant never outlives the picture it was given for; across
  sessions the explicit deactivation above is what revokes.
- **Challenge → phone.** Each `onGrantChallenge` (while control is active:
  at once, then every 2 s), while the session runs and is paired, goes to
  the viewer as `screen-helper-challenge` with the current run's `epoch`.
  A malformed one (the helper's pipe admits any process of the PC user) is
  never forwarded. Not in `channelState()`: a challenge lives 6 s and the
  next comes sooner.
- **Grant → helper.** A `screen-helper-grant` is relayed with `sendGrant`
  only when its `epoch` is the current run and the session runs and is
  paired; otherwise it is dropped (the helper would refuse it anyway).
- **Issues.** `onHelperIssue` codes in `REMOTE_SCREEN_HELPER_ISSUES`
  (`screenHelperIssue`) become the status's `issue` while this session has
  the helper active; other codes are not the phone's (handshake failures
  close the connection; a refused grant is followed by the next
  challenge). An issue ends when the helper is deactivated (its own lapse
  report after that is ignored), at a helper change (connect, desktop
  switch, disconnect, rebuild: `helperIssueAfterChange`; `desktop_unavailable`
  ends at the next `desktop-changed` per the spec) except
  `grant_key_missing`, which describes the install and stands while
  connected, and `grant_expired` once the next grant for the run was relayed.
- **`secure`** in the block is the decision's reason when it is `lock` or
  `uac`, else null.

### PC access: install and enroll moments

"PC access" (접근 권한) is the secure-desktop service as the user meets it.
Installing it and enrolling a phone's controller key need admin rights, so each happens at a
moment when someone can approve it:

- **Key delivery at pairing** (`renderer/remote-shim-pairing.ts`,
  `shared/remote-controller-key.ts`, `main/remote-controller-keys.ts`). Once
  an approved connection's E2EE channel is up, the phone makes this pairing's
  controller key (`ensureControllerKey`) and calls
  `deliverScreenControllerKey([publicKey])` over that channel. The PC's
  method table is served only from frames decrypted on an established
  channel. It binds the key to the relay credential that leg authenticated,
  never to a request field, and refuses a connection with no credential, a
  device whose unpair is recorded, or a value that isn't a P-256 point. The
  key is kept with the paired-device record (`remote-client-cache.ts`,
  `controllerKeys`) and goes with that device's confirmed unpair or a
  reset. Nothing is elevated at pairing. Each accepted delivery (every
  connection delivers again) is announced to the desktop app as the
  `remote-controller-key-delivered` event, which enrolls it (below).
- **Computer Use setup on the PC** (`main/pc-access.ts`, the Windows row of
  `renderer/settings/computer-readiness.ts`). The Readiness section's last
  row, *PC access for admin prompts and the lock screen*, is optional and
  never blocks Computer Use. Each of its actions is one ordinary UAC prompt
  (the person is at the PC), through the one shared
  `secureDesktopInstallerFor` installer:
  - not installed (or outdated): **Approve** runs
    `install(keys of every paired phone that delivered one, {revoke: pending})`.
    The install writes exactly those keys (possibly none) and records the
    app-delegation policy, so later phones need no prompt;
  - installed, and a missing phone's delegated enroll (or the pending
    revoke before it) was refused in a way only elevation fixes
    (`delegation-disabled`, `delegation-denied`): **Approve new phone** runs
    one UAC `enroll(missing keys, {revoke: pending})`. The bridge applies the
    revokes and the enrolls in one key-set write, so both commit or neither.
    The row stays hidden while a delegated enroll is in flight and after
    `service-unreachable` (the phone's next delivery tries again);
  - installed, but the revocations owed are unknown (below): **Approve**
    reinstalls, `install(keys of the current pairings, {revoke: pending})`;
  - nothing to approve: no row;
  - another Windows account owns it: an informational row, no action.

  Whether a key is enrolled is the bridge's `check --controller-key`:
  `installed` while that key is enrolled in a current install, `not-enrolled`
  (exit 7) when the current install lacks it.
- **A phone paired after setup** is enrolled by the desktop app on its key
  delivery: `enroll(key, {delegated: true})`, unelevated through the
  service's delegation pipe, with no PC prompt (the service shows its own
  notification). Only a phone paired now is enrolled (its record present and
  not unpaired). Nothing happens while the service is not installed for this
  account. Every pending revoke is first applied through delegation; if one
  does not run, or the revocations are unknown, nothing is enrolled.
- **From the phone with a Windows password** (the fallback when nobody is at
  the PC; no UAC prompt). The blocked secure-screen view's button ("Approve PC
  access", or "Approve access again" for an update) opens a bottom sheet with
  one password field (design/mockups/remote-screen-helper-install). The
  account field appears only when the PC says its signed-in account is not an
  administrator: `helperInfo.accountIsAdmin` (optional on the wire; absent, an
  older PC or a failed check, means the password only). The PC reads it from
  the process token's groups (`whoami /groups`, `main/secure-desktop/
  account-admin.ts`), once per run. Submit sends `screen-helper-install` (an
  `install` offer) or `screen-helper-enroll` (an `update` offer) with
  `credential: {password, user?}` (`user` only when the account field was
  shown); the PC treats both kinds the same, since it decides install or enroll
  from its own state. The password field is emptied by every submit.
  - **Routed through PC access.** `viewer.ts` hands a message with a
    `credential` to `helperCredential`, then `RemoteScreenSource.
    requestHelperCredential` (running and paired only; one request at a time
    per session; the install's extra `keys` are ignored), then
    `PcAccess.approveWithCredential` in the same serialized queue as Approve.
    It is `approve` with the credential in place of UAC and nothing else
    changed: not installed (or outdated, or the revocations unknown) →
    `install(keys of the current pairings, {revoke: pending, credential})`;
    installed with phones missing → `enroll(missing, {revoke: pending,
    credential})`; nothing missing → `enrolled`. The owed revocations are
    taken over first, the pending record is cleared only by a successful call,
    and one password request at a time is accepted PC-wide (another is
    answered `busy`, not queued: nothing ran, the offer stands, and the
    phone shows a "try again in a moment" line and keeps its button; unlike
    `in-progress`, which is a prompt open on the PC). The request is refused (`failed`)
    unless the session's client is a phone paired now whose delivered key is
    exactly the one sent, and not one awaiting revocation.
  - **The answer** is `helperInfo.outcome` (`installed`, `updated`,
    `enrolled`, or `bad-credentials`, `not-admin`, `logon-type-denied`,
    `account-locked`, `account-disabled`, `policy-blocked`, `failed`, …) with
    the offer relative to the phone's key, pushed even when it equals the last
    status (a wrong password twice reads the same twice). The phone shows the
    fixed copy for it inside the sheet and keeps the sheet for a refusal.
  - **The password** rides the verified, encrypted channel, is bounded
    (`CREDUI_MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH`, `CREDUI_MAX_USERNAME_LENGTH`), goes to the
    bridge's stdin only (`runSecureDesktopWithLogon`), is never logged,
    persisted or echoed in any message, and the source empties its copy once
    the call ended.
- **Unpair on the PC** (Settings → Connection → Remove) is one transaction
  in the same queue as every enrollment, approval and revoke, so no
  delivery or drain runs in the middle of it. The phone's key is read and
  written to the app's pending-revoke file (`pc-access-revokes.json` in user
  data) before the unpair runs; if it cannot be written, the unpair fails
  with that error. An unreadable key marks the revocations unknown instead.
  The unpair then runs, and its answer returns. Still inside the
  transaction, `revoke(key, {delegated: true})` runs; only a confirmed
  `revoked` removes the key from the file. Every other outcome, a throw, a
  failed unpair, or quitting mid-revoke keeps it (each refusal logged by its
  outcome). A pending revoke is passed with the next UAC install or enroll
  and tried through delegation before the next delegated enroll.
- **Every pairing removal in the service** (an unpair from any caller,
  Disconnect all's rotation, the recovery reset after lost revocation
  records) owes the removed phones' controller keys in `remote-clients.json`
  (`owedAccessKeys`, `remote-client-cache.ts` `oweAccess`) before any pairing
  or key mapping goes: `queueRevoke`, `applied` and `clear` owe in the same
  write that unpairs or forgets a device, and rotation and recovery owe every
  mapped key first. A paired phone that delivers a different key (after
  clearing its app data) has the replaced key owed in the same write that
  stores the new one, so it is revoked before the new key enrolls; the same
  key again owes nothing. A damaged client record lost the keys, so its owed
  revocations are unknown (`owedAccessUnknown`). The service then sends
  `remote-controller-keys-owed`. The desktop app takes the owed keys over
  (into its pending file, durably, then settles them in the service) before
  every delivery, approval and revoke, and revokes them on that event.
- **The rule: a revocation is never lost, and a pending one blocks every new
  enrollment.** The pending file holds at most 256 keys (the pairing cap).
  A missing file is empty. A damaged, wrong-shaped or unreadable one is
  copied aside as `pc-access-revokes.json.damaged-<marker>` and replaced by
  an "unknown" record, as is a full one on the next add. While revocations
  are unknown nothing is enrolled; the next elevated install, which writes
  the full key set from the current pairings, resolves it (a loss recorded
  while that install ran stays unknown).
- **No automatic request.** A phone screen session never asks for the helper
  by itself; only the phone's password sheet (opened by the blocked-state
  button) sends `screen-helper-install` or `screen-helper-enroll`.

### Helper video

While the helper serves, the phone sees its frames instead of the desktop
capture (which shows the last ordinary frame there). The source reports the
switch as `videoPath()` / `onVideoPath` (`capture` | `helper`, from the
decision), and the screen's WebRTC adapter (`screen-webrtc-source.ts`) drives
the sender:

- **Mechanism: the same peer connection, another track.** On `helper` the
  adapter calls `sink.drawnTrack(key, true)`; the host sends `source-draw` and
  the sender replaces the source's capture track with a canvas-drawn one
  (`captureStream(0)`, a frame per drawn picture) on every connection with
  `RTCRtpSender.replaceTrack`. No renegotiation: the connection, its
  channel, its codec and the phone's geometry stay as they are. Each helper
  frame goes through the host's picture feed (newest only, one in flight per
  source, superseded ones dropped) as raw rows (`image/x-bgrx`).
- **No pixel work in main.** `screenFrameRegion` only locates the display in
  the helper frame (which covers the whole virtual screen): the rows that
  cover it (a view of the helper's buffer, so the rows above and below are
  never forwarded), the source rectangle within them, and where it lands in
  the locked picture. A frame superseded in the queue costs nothing; only
  the picture actually sent is copied into an array of its own (a memcpy of
  those rows, since the IPC would otherwise serialize the view's whole
  buffer). The sender wraps the rows in a WebCodecs `VideoFrame`
  (`format: 'BGRX'`, the helper's own byte order, with its stride), fills
  the canvas black and draws the source rectangle onto the target one
  (`drawImage`, high-quality smoothing): crop, scale and colour conversion
  all run in Chromium. Why raw rows rather than an encoded image: the
  helper already hands over raw BGRA, and an encode in main would cost the
  window process's main thread per frame.
- **Rate.** No byte-rate budget is derived: there is no measured figure for
  Electron's main → renderer IPC throughput to derive one from. The rate is
  capped by the stream's own frame rate instead: at most one helper picture
  per `1000 / maxFrameRate` ms (30 fps: 33.3 ms) is handed over. The helper
  is slower still (one frame per 66 ms at most, and only once its previous
  one was written out), and the host keeps one picture in flight per
  source, so at most one frame's rows cross the IPC at a time.
- **Geometry.** The target is the locked geometry's pixel size, so the track
  keeps its resolution and the generation does not change. Desktop area the
  frame doesn't cover stays black. A display change while the helper serves
  locks a new geometry as always (new generation, the frames follow it);
  the capture plan's reopen waits until the capture is back.

#### Video runs and control

Every path change, every pipeline stall and every loss of the viewer's
channel (demote, viewer left: `release`) starts a new **video run**: its
`epoch` increases, everything of the old run stops counting, and control on
the helper path is withdrawn (held input released) until the new run earns
it. The phone hears each run as `screen-video` (see "Contract fold-in"); a
capture run at once, a helper run only once its first frame is in the track,
so frames sent after the announcement belong to the new run.
`channelState()` carries the current run once it was announced.

Control on the helper path needs, for the current run, both:

- **Local delivery** (`delivered(epoch)`). Each picture carries its run's
  epoch. The sender answers it with `frame-done`; `ok` means it was drawn
  into the source's current track after that track was on every sender
  (`installed`), and the host passes the picture's epoch on. A switch of the
  track (`drawnTrack`) drops the picture in flight, so its late
  acknowledgement matches nothing; a delivery of another run is ignored.
  This is evidence about this PC's pipeline only.
- **Receipt** (`frameSeen(epoch)`): the phone's `screen-frame-seen` for the
  run, routed by the viewer from the channel (not input: never gated by the
  input epoch, never acked). A seen of another run, or one before the run
  was announced, is ignored. The phone side is built separately; until it
  sends it, there is no control on the helper path, which is the safe
  default.

**Pipeline watchdog** (`helperVideoStallMs`): with no delivery of the run
for `max(3 × average, average + 150 ms)`, the average over its last 30
delivery intervals (216 ms at the helper's nominal 66 ms before there are
two), the run ends. The threshold borrows the shape of the webrtc-stats
freeze rule (`freezeCount`) but applies it to local deliveries: it watches
main → the sender's track, not the network or the phone's renderer, which
